content: Routine care for women, excluding those referred for specialized care, should adhere to the guidelines outlined in this document. Scheduled visits, including routine and follow-up appointments, are conducted during regular office hours. Emergency services, which include unscheduled visits for labor, delivery, complications, or severe illness, are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Women and newborns experiencing complications or anticipated complications are referred to secondary-level care facilities, such as referral hospitals, for further management. The referral and transportation process must be appropriate for the distance and circumstances involved. Some deliveries occur at home, attended by traditional birth attendants (TBAs), relatives, or the woman herself. However, home deliveries without a skilled attendant are not recommended. Connections with the community and traditional providers are established to ensure comprehensive care. Primary healthcare services and community involvement are integral to addressing maternal and newborn health issues. Other program activities, such as managing malaria, tuberculosis, and other lung diseases, providing HIV treatment, and offering infant feeding counseling, require specialized training and are delivered by different providers either at the same facility or at referral hospitals. Skilled attendants are responsible for detecting, initiating treatment, and referring cases as needed. All pregnant women are routinely offered HIV testing and counseling during their first contact with a healthcare worker, which may occur during antenatal visits, early labor, or the postpartum period. Women first seen in late labor are offered testing after childbirth. Healthcare workers are trained to provide HIV testing and counseling, and HIV testing kits and antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are available at primary healthcare facilities. The guide assumes that professionals using it possess the necessary knowledge and skills to provide the described care. Additional training materials should be utilized to ensure the required competency level. Communication with women and their companions should be welcoming, friendly, respectful, and non-judgmental. Simple and clear language should be used, and women should be encouraged to ask questions. Information should be tailored to their needs, and they should be supported in understanding their options and making decisions. Before any examination or procedure, permission must be sought, and the woman should be informed about what is being done. Key information, including details about routine laboratory tests and treatments, should be summarized, and the woman’s understanding of emergency signs, treatment instructions, and follow-up plans should be verified. Privacy and confidentiality must be maintained in all interactions with women and their partners. Examinations and counseling should be conducted in private settings, and sensitive discussions should not be overheard. Consent must be obtained before discussing matters with the woman’s partner or family. Confidential information about clients should not be shared with other providers or outside the healthcare facility. Examination areas should be organized to protect the woman’s privacy, and all records must be kept confidential and securely stored. When prescribing or recommending treatments and preventive measures for the woman or her baby, the healthcare provider should explain the purpose and benefits of the treatment, emphasizing that it will not harm the woman or her baby and that not taking it may pose greater risks. Clear instructions on how to take the medication regularly should be provided, and the procedure should be demonstrated if necessary. The provider should explain how the treatment is administered to the baby and discuss potential side effects, reassuring the woman that they are not serious and providing guidance on managing them. Women should be advised to return if they encounter any problems or concerns with the treatment. Barriers to treatment adherence should be explored, and any misinformation should be clarified. The importance of purchasing and taking the prescribed amount should be emphasized. Service hours should be clearly posted, and appointments should be kept on time. If delays occur, women should be informed. Before beginning services, equipment should be checked for cleanliness and functionality, and supplies and drugs should be in place. The facility should be kept clean through regular cleaning. At the end of the service, waste and sharps should be safely discarded, equipment and supplies should be cleaned and disinfected, linen should be replaced and prepared for washing, supplies and drugs should be replenished, and routine cleaning of all areas should be ensured. Daily and occasional administrative activities include maintaining records of equipment, supplies, drugs, and vaccines, checking the availability and functionality of essential equipment, and ordering stocks before they run out. Staffing lists and schedules should be established. Clinical findings, treatments, reasons for referral, and follow-up recommendations should always be recorded in clinical and home-based records at the time of observation. Confidential information should not be recorded in home-based records if the woman is unwilling. The health facility must comply with international conventions, such as the International Code of Marketing of Breast Milk Substitutes, and should not distribute free or low-cost supplies or products within its scope. Standard precautions and cleanliness must be observed to protect women, babies, and healthcare providers from infections, including HIV. Hands should be washed with soap and water before and after caring for a woman or newborn, before any treatment procedure, and whenever contaminated with blood or body fluids. Gloves should be worn during procedures such as vaginal examinations, delivery, cord cutting, and handling contaminated waste. Protective measures, such as wearing aprons and eye protection, should be taken during deliveries to prevent exposure to blood and body fluids. Safe disposal of sharps and waste is essential, and contaminated laundry should be handled separately and washed appropriately. Instruments that penetrate the skin must be sterilized or disposed of after single use, and all equipment in contact with intact skin should be thoroughly cleaned or disinfected. Visits should be organized to ensure immediate reception and response to women and newborns seeking care. A quick check should be performed on all incoming women and babies, and emergency assessment and management should begin at the first sign of an emergency. Women in labor should be accompanied to an appropriate place, and steps for childbirth care should be followed. Women with priority signs should be examined immediately, and those without emergency or priority signs should be invited to wait in the waiting room. Newborns who appear small should be examined immediately without delay. During emergency care visits, the healthcare provider should introduce themselves, ask the woman’s name, and encourage her companion to stay with her. Procedures should be explained, permission should be sought, and the woman should be kept informed. Privacy should be respected during examinations and discussions. If the woman is accompanied by a baby who is well, the companion should be asked to care for the baby during the maternal examination and treatment. When a woman or baby is referred to a secondary-level care facility for specific problems or complications, the guide assumes that the referral facility will assess, treat, counsel, and provide follow-up advice for the condition. Follow-up care may be organized by the referral facility, or written instructions may be provided for the skilled attendant at the primary level. Women and babies should be advised to return for a follow-up visit within two weeks, depending on the severity of the condition. Routine visits should begin with a warm greeting, offering the woman a seat, and introducing oneself. The woman’s name and the baby’s name should be asked, and the purpose of the visit should be clarified. If the woman is recently delivered, the baby should be assessed or seen if not present with the mother. For antenatal care, the birth plan should be revised at the end of the visit. For postpartum visits, the baby should also be examined. Follow-up visits within a week should focus on the specific condition requiring follow-up, while visits more than a week after the initial examination should include a full assessment as required for antenatal, post-abortion, postpartum, or newborn care. During the visit, all procedures should be explained, permission should be sought before examinations or tests, and the woman should be kept informed throughout. Findings should be discussed with the woman and her partner, and privacy should be ensured during examinations and discussions. At the end of the visit, the woman should be asked if she has any questions, and the most important messages should be summarized. She should be encouraged to return for routine visits and informed about when to return. The Home-Based Maternal Record (HBMR) should be completed, and the appropriate information sheet should be provided to the woman.
